stories.title: Night Night, Little Farm
stories.summary: A soft, repeating goodnight to the cow, the hen, the pig, and the moon over a sleepy farm.
paragraphs: The sun goes down on the little farm. Down, down, down.
Night night, cow. Moo, moo, moo. The cow lies down in the soft, soft hay.
Night night, hen. Cluck, cluck, cluck. The hen tucks her head under her warm, warm wing.
Night night, pig. Oink, oink, oink. The pig snuggles in the cozy, cozy straw.
Night night, sheep. Baa, baa, baa. The sheep curls up, fluffy and round.
Up comes the moon. Hello, moon. Shh, shh, shh.
The stars come out, twinkle, twinkle. The barn is quiet. The farm is sleepy.
Night night, little farm. And night night, little you.

stories.title: The Littlest Pumpkin's Lantern
stories.summary: A small pumpkin on a quiet porch learns her soft glow is just right for helping a sleepy moth find home.
paragraphs: On a quiet porch at the end of a quiet street, there sat a row of pumpkins. There was a big round pumpkin, a tall bumpy pumpkin, and one very little pumpkin named Pip.

When the sky turned the color of blueberry jam, someone came and placed a candle inside each pumpkin. The big round pumpkin glowed bright and orange. The tall bumpy pumpkin glowed warm and gold. Pip glowed too, but only a little. Just a soft, small glow, like a nightlight.
"My light is so small," Pip whispered. "Nobody will even notice it."

Just then, flutter, flutter, flutter, a tiny gray moth drifted down from the trees. She was yawning a very big moth yawn. "Oh dear," said the moth. "The big lights are so bright, I can't see where my leaf bed is. I'm so sleepy."
Pip thought for a moment. Then Pip glowed her softest, gentlest glow. In that little light, the moth could see the garden path, the curly vine, and right there, a cozy folded leaf, just her size.
"There it is," sighed the moth. "Thank you, little pumpkin. Your light is just right."
The moth tucked herself into her leaf bed. The big round pumpkin smiled. The tall bumpy pumpkin smiled. And Pip smiled the warmest smile of all.
One by one, the porch lights went out. The street grew quiet. And Pip kept her small, soft glow, just right, all through the sleepy night.

stories.title: Otto and the Cloud Ferry
stories.summary: A curious otter rides a fluffy cloud ferry across the night sky to deliver a lost star back home.
paragraphs: Otto the otter lived in a snug burrow beside a silver river. Every night, before bed, he floated on his back and looked up at the stars. He liked to count them. He always got to one hundred and then fell asleep, so he never knew how many there were.

One evening, as Otto floated and counted, something small and sparkly drifted down and landed on his tummy with a soft little plink. It was a star. A tiny one, no bigger than a pebble, glowing a sleepy yellow.
"Oh," said the star in a voice like a little bell. "I rolled off the edge of the sky. Now I can't get home."
Otto held the star carefully in his paws. "Don't worry," he said. "We'll find a way."

Just then, a puffy cloud floated low over the river. It had a little round window and a little round door, and a sign that said Cloud Ferry. A friendly heron in a captain's hat leaned out. "All aboard for the night sky," she called softly. "Last trip of the evening."

Otto climbed in, holding the star close. The cloud was soft as a pillow and smelled a little like rain. Slowly, gently, the ferry rose up, up, up, past the treetops, past a sleepy owl who blinked hello, past the hills that looked like big folded blankets.
The higher they went, the quieter it got. The wind hummed a low, slow tune. The river below became a thin silver ribbon. Otto could see his burrow, tiny as a button, with its little door.
At last they reached the dark velvet sky, where all the stars were twinkling. Right in the middle of a star pattern shaped like a teapot, there was one empty spot.

"That's my place," said the little star happily. Otto stretched up on his tiptoes and placed the star right where it belonged. It gave a happy twinkle, and the whole teapot shape glowed a little brighter, as if it were saying thank you.

The heron turned the cloud ferry around, and down they drifted, slow and soft, all the way back to the riverbank. Otto thanked the captain and padded into his burrow. He curled up in his bed of moss, tail wrapped around his nose.

Through his little window he could see the teapot of stars, with one tiny star winking at him. Otto began to count, one, two, three. He got all the way to eleven before his eyes closed, and he was fast asleep.
